claim: El Hage et al. (2018) reported that the unliganded hemoglobin protein is only stable in the T state when a solvent box is used in the simulations that is ten times larger than what is usually employed.
source: A recent molecular dynamics investigation into the stability of hemoglobin concluded that the unliganded protein is only stable in the T state when a solvent box is used in the simulations that is ten times larger than what is usually employed (El Hage et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to El Hage et al., 2018.

claim: El Hage et al. (2018) reported that the T state was stable for a period of 1 microsecond only in a relatively large simulation box with a cube edge length of 15 nm.
source: It was reported that the T state was stable for a period of 1 microsecond only in a relatively large simulation box with a cube edge length of 15 nm, whereas in smaller simulation boxes spontaneous transitions to the R state were observed on this timescale.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to El Hage et al., 2018 in the context.

claim: El Hage et al. (2018) reported that in smaller simulation boxes spontaneous transitions to the R state were observed on the 1 microsecond timescale.
source: It was reported that the T state was stable for a period of 1 microsecond only in a relatively large simulation box with a cube edge length of 15 nm, whereas in smaller simulation boxes spontaneous transitions to the R state were observed on this timescale.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to El Hage et al., 2018 in the context.

claim: El Hage et al. (2018) attributed thermodynamic stabilization of the T state in the larger box to a change in the hydrophobic effect due to a change in the box size.
source: Based on this, thermodynamic stabilization of the T state in the larger box was concluded, attributed to a change in the hydrophobic effect due to a change in the box size.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to El Hage et al., 2018 in the context.

claim: In the work by El Hage et al., for each of the four studied box sizes, a single MD simulation was carried out.
source: First, in the work by El Hage et al. for each of the four studied box sizes, a single MD simulation was carried out and a transition (or lack thereof) was reported.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the El Hage et al. study.

claim: The El Hage et al. (2018) study lacks an estimate of the uncertainty in the reported transition times.
source: Based on the single data points, an estimate of the uncertainty in the reported transition times is lacking, impairing an assessment of the statistical significance of the observed differences.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the El Hage et al. study.

claim: The statistical significance of the concluded box size dependence in El Hage et al. (2018) has not been shown.
source: The statistical significance of the concluded box size dependence has thus not been shown.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the El Hage et al. study.

claim: There is considerable scatter in the transition times obtained in single MD simulations when redoing the simulations presented by El Hage et al. (2018) using multiple replicas.
source: In redoing the simulations presented by El Hage et al. (2018) using multiple replicas (20 for the 9 and 15 nm setup, 10 for the 12 nm setup, we find that there is considerable scatter in the transition times obtained in single MD simulations (see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own simulations shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the 9 nm box, a substantial fraction of simulations does not undergo the T to R transition within 1 µs.
source: For example, we find that in the 9 nm box a substantial fraction does not undergo the transition within 1 µs, rendering the absence of a transition in the single simulation of the 15 nm box in the El Hage et al. (2018) study statistically insignificantly different from those observed for the 9 nm box.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own simulations.

claim: Out of 20 simulations for the 15 nm system, 11 made the transition within 400 ns and 14 within 1 µs.
source: This is further underscored by the fact that out of 20 simulations we set up for the 15 nm system, 11 made the transition within 400 ns and 14 within 1 µs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own simulations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The distributions of RMSD values to the T and R state crystal structures monitored at 400 ns and 1 µs of simulation time are highly similar for the studied box sizes.
source: Consistent with this result, we find that the distributions of RMSD values to the T and R state crystal structures monitored at 400 ns and 1 µs of simulation time are highly similar for the studied box sizes (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own simulations shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The probability of a factor of 2 slower kinetics in the 15 nm box amounts to 0.0026.
source: Specifically, we have estimated the probability of a slowdown in the 15 nm box, as claimed by El Hage et al. (2018). For a relatively moderate effect of a factor of 2 slower kinetics, this amounts to a probability of 0.0026, for a factor of 10 it amounts to 4.7e-6.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the authors' simulation data.

claim: The probability of a factor of 10 slower kinetics in the 15 nm box amounts to 4.7e-6.
source: Specifically, we have estimated the probability of a slowdown in the 15 nm box, as claimed by El Hage et al. (2018). For a relatively moderate effect of a factor of 2 slower kinetics, this amounts to a probability of 0.0026, for a factor of 10 it amounts to 4.7e-6.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the authors' simulation data.

claim: The box size dependence hypothesis can be rejected with a relatively large statistical margin.
source: We can thus reject the box size dependence hypothesis with a relatively large statistical margin.
evidence: This claim is based on the statistical analysis of the authors' simulation data.

claim: No full back-transition to the T state after a T to R transition was observed in any of the simulated systems using the El Hage et al. simulation setup.
source: We have not observed a full back-transition in any of the simulated systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own simulations.

claim: Occasional partial transitions back to the T state are observed, independent of the box size.
source: We only observe occasional partial transitions back to the T state (see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1), independent of the box size.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' own simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no detectable stabilization of the T state over the R state in the 15 nm box.
source: This is consistent with the finding above that there is no detectable stabilization of the T state over the R state in the 15 nm box.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' simulation data.

claim: When solvent radial distribution function is normalized based on the analysis volume rather than by the box volume, no significant box size effect is found.
source: Indeed, if we reanalyze the solvent radial distribution function (Figure 2A) or water-water hydrogen bonds (Figure 2B) and normalize based on the analysis volume (which we keep constant for the differently sized boxes) rather than by the box volume as was done originally, we find no significant box size effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' reanalysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When water-water hydrogen bonds are normalized based on the analysis volume rather than by the box volume, no significant box size effect is found.
source: Indeed, if we reanalyze the solvent radial distribution function (Figure 2A) or water-water hydrogen bonds (Figure 2B) and normalize based on the analysis volume (which we keep constant for the differently sized boxes) rather than by the box volume as was done originally, we find no significant box size effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' reanalysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A dilution effect is observed for the diffusion constant due to different ratio of protein to water in differently sized boxes.
source: A similar dilution effect is observed for the diffusion constant. Averaging over the complete box represents a weighted average over restricted and bulk waters. For larger boxes, more water molecules are unrestricted by the protein and therefore behave bulk-like, yielding a larger weight of bulk water to the average.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the analysis of diffusion constants.

claim: The diffusion constants obtained by reweighting with the additional number of water molecules in the larger boxes are remarkably close to the ones originally computed for the 12 and 15 nm sized boxes.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2C, the resulting diffusion constants obtained this way are remarkably close to the ones originally computed for the 12 and 15 nm sized boxes, indicating that the observed differences in average diffusion constant can be largely explained by the dilution effect and thus do not reflect a box size effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The observed differences in average diffusion constant can be largely explained by the dilution effect and thus do not reflect a box size effect.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2C, the resulting diffusion constants obtained this way are remarkably close to the ones originally computed for the 12 and 15 nm sized boxes, indicating that the observed differences in average diffusion constant can be largely explained by the dilution effect and thus do not reflect a box size effect.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Yeh and Hummer, 2004 showed that the box size dependence on water diffusion is small for box sizes larger than 4 nm.
source: This is consistent with earlier results from Yeh and Hummer, 2004 who showed that the box size dependence on water diffusion is small for box sizes larger than 4 nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yeh and Hummer, 2004.

claim: Ubiquitin is significantly smaller than hemoglobin.
source: Note that ubiquitin is significantly smaller than hemoglobin and therefore the hydrophobic effect should be expected to be significantly smaller, following the argumentation of El Hage et al. (2018).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about protein sizes.

claim: The hydrophobic effect in ubiquitin should be expected to be significantly smaller than in hemoglobin, following the argumentation of El Hage et al. (2018).
source: Note that ubiquitin is significantly smaller than hemoglobin and therefore the hydrophobic effect should be expected to be significantly smaller, following the argumentation of El Hage et al. (2018).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the argumentation of El Hage et al. (2018).

claim: A similar box size effect on the (unnormalized) RDF and diffusion constant is observed in ubiquitin as in hemoglobin, confirming that the underlying cause is the dilution effect rather than a box size effect on the hydrophobic effect.
source: The fact that nevertheless we see a similar box size effect on the (unnormalized) RDF and diffusion constant confirms that the underlying cause is the dilution effect rather than a box size effect on the hydrophobic effect.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inherent, unavoidable dilution effect associated with increasing the box size is sufficient to explain the observed data.
source: As the inherent, unavoidable dilution effect associated with increasing the box size is sufficient to explain the observed data, this implies there is no evidence to justify assuming an additional effect on protein solvation or the hydrophobic effect.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' analysis.

claim: There is no evidence to justify assuming an additional effect on protein solvation or the hydrophobic effect beyond the dilution effect.
source: As the inherent, unavoidable dilution effect associated with increasing the box size is sufficient to explain the observed data, this implies there is no evidence to justify assuming an additional effect on protein solvation or the hydrophobic effect.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' analysis.

claim: The dilution effect removes the justification for Figures 3, 4 and 5 of El Hage et al. (2018).
source: This thus removes the justification for Figures 3, 4 and 5 of El Hage et al. (2018).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' analysis.

claim: The current data do not indicate that protein solvation or the hydrophobic effect changes significantly with the simulation box size for the studied range.
source: It is important to note that this does not preclude the hydrophobic effect hypothesis: however, the current data do not indicate that protein solvation or the hydrophobic effect changes significantly with the simulation box size for the studied range.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' analysis.

claim: According to rate theory, the transition times are primarily related to the activation barrier and the attempt frequency of the transition.
source: According to rate theory, the transition times are primarily related to the activation barrier and the attempt frequency of the transition.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from rate theory.

claim: Longer transition times could either be caused by a lowering of the attempt frequency or an increased barrier.
source: Therefore, longer transition times could either be caused by a lowering of the attempt frequency or an increased barrier.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from rate theory.

claim: An increased barrier can be achieved by a higher thermodynamic stability or by solely increasing the barrier and thus leaving the thermodynamic equilibrium between T and R unaltered.
source: In turn, an increased barrier (e.g. to leave the T state) can be achieved by a higher thermodynamic stability (lowering the well of the T state) but equally well by solely increasing the barrier and thus leaving the thermodynamic equlibrium between T and R unaltered.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from rate theory.

claim: Without addressing the barrier and the attempt frequency, transition times to leave a state are insufficient to draw conclusions about the thermodynamic stability of that state.
source: Without addressing the barrier and the attempt frequency, transition times to leave a state are thus insufficient to draw conclusions about the thermodynamic stability of that state.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from rate theory.

claim: The presented transition times in El Hage et al. report primarily on the kinetics of the T to R transition rather than the thermodynamic difference between the T and R states.
source: We thus argue that the presented transition times report primarily on the kinetics of the T to R transition rather than the thermodynamic difference between the T and R states.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from rate theory.

claim: Spontaneous transitions towards the R state were observed under each of the simulated conditions for deoxy hemoglobin.
source: Spontaneous transitions towards the R state were observed under each of the simulated conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Histidine protonation states as used by Hub et al. (2010) were found to lead to generally faster transitions than histidine protonation as suggested by Kovalevsky et al., 2010.
source: Histidine protonation states as used by Hub et al. (2010) were found to lead to generally faster transitions than histidine protonation as suggested by Kovalevsky et al., 2010, in line with earlier simulations using the GROMOS96 43A1 force field (Van Gunsteren et al., 1996; Vesper and de Groot, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations and citations to earlier work.

claim: The finding that histidine protonation states as used by Hub et al. (2010) lead to generally faster transitions than histidine protonation as suggested by Kovalevsky et al., 2010 is in line with earlier simulations using the GROMOS96 43A1 force field (Van Gunsteren et al., 1996; Vesper and de Groot, 2013).
source: Histidine protonation states as used by Hub et al. (2010) were found to lead to generally faster transitions than histidine protonation as suggested by Kovalevsky et al., 2010, in line with earlier simulations using the GROMOS96 43A1 force field (Van Gunsteren et al., 1996; Vesper and de Groot, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to earlier work.

claim: The setup of El Hage et al. leads to generally slower transitions than either of the Hub et al. (2010) or Kovalevsky et al., 2010 protonation states.
source: Interestingly, the setup of El Hage et al. leads to generally slower transitions than either of these two protonation states.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations.

claim: No dependence on the simulation box size was observed for the transition times for any of the tested setups.
source: No dependence on the simulation box size was observed for the transition times for any of the tested setups (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The histidine protonation states in the El Hage et al. setup were virtually identical to the Hub et al. (2010) setup and therefore are unlikely responsible for the slower transition times.
source: In a preliminary investigation into the cause of the generally slower transitions in the El Hage et al. setup, we noted that the histidine protonation states were virtually identical to the Hub et al. (2010) setup and therefore are unlikely responsible for the slower transition times.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' analysis.

claim: The only difference in protonation state between El Hage et al. and Hub et al. (2010) setups concerns His72, which is protonated on the delta position in both α subunits in the Hub setup, whereas it is protonated on the delta position on the α−1 subunit and on the epsilon position on the α−2 subunit in the El Hage et al. setup.
source: The only difference in protonation state concerns His72, which is protonated on the delta position in both α subunits in the Hub setup, whereas it is protonated on the delta position on the α−1 subunit and on the epsilon position on the α−2 subunit in the El Hage et al. setup.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the simulation setups.

claim: Since α-His72 is exposed to the solvent, its protonation is unlikely to affect the T to R transition.
source: Since α-His72 is exposed to the solvent, its protonation is unlikely to affect the T to R transition.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural considerations.

claim: In the Hub et al. (2010) and Vesper and de Groot, 2013 setups a covalent bond was modeled between the iron and the epsilon nitrogen of the proximal histidine for all four subunits, whereas this interaction was modeled with non-bonded interactions in the El Hage et al. (2018) setup.
source: Second, whereas in the Hub et al. (2010) and Vesper and de Groot, 2013 setups a covalent bond was modeled between the iron and the epsilon nitrogen of the proximal histidine for all four subunits, this interaction was modeled with non-bonded interactions in the El Hage et al. (2018) setup.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the simulation setups.

claim: Based on the current data, the box geometry does not appear to have a major effect on transition kinetics, but more systematic analyses would be required for a definitive answer.
source: Based on the current data, the box geometry does not appear to have a major effect, but more systematic analyses would be required for a definitive answer.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' data with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: No systematic effect of the box size on the transition kinetics was observed for alanine dipeptide and ubiquitin.
source: Also for these systems, no systematic effect of the box size on the transition kinetics was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Only minor effects, if any, of the box size on the obtained free energy profiles were observed for alanine dipeptide, ubiquitin and the pentapeptide RGGGD.
source: For the three systems, only minor effects, if any, of the box size on the obtained free energy profiles were observed (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: With an order of magnitude more statistics, the reported box size dependence is not reproducible.
source: In addition, we find that with an order of magnitude more statistics, the reported box size dependence is not reproducible.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations.

claim: No significant effects on the kinetics or thermodynamics of conformational transitions were observed due to box size.
source: Overall, no significant effects on the kinetics or thermodynamics of conformational transitions were observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations.

claim: The observation of El Hage et al. (2018) that the stability of hemoglobin in the T state in the largest box of 15 nm was not significantly different from the other investigated box sizes.
source: In conclusion, we have shown that the observation of El Hage et al. (2018) that the stability of hemoglobin in the T state in the largest box of 15 nm was not significantly different from the other investigated box sizes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations.

claim: The results from hemoglobin simulations indicate that under the simulated conditions the R state is favored over the T state.
source: The results from hemoglobin simulations indicate that under the simulated conditions the R state is favored over the T state, with the histidine protonation states affecting the transition statistics, consistent with the Bohr effect (Zheng et al., 2013) and previous simulations (Hub et al., 2010; Vesper and de Groot, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations and citations to earlier work.

claim: The histidine protonation states affect the transition statistics in hemoglobin, consistent with the Bohr effect (Zheng et al., 2013) and previous simulations (Hub et al., 2010; Vesper and de Groot, 2013).
source: The results from hemoglobin simulations indicate that under the simulated conditions the R state is favored over the T state, with the histidine protonation states affecting the transition statistics, consistent with the Bohr effect (Zheng et al., 2013) and previous simulations (Hub et al., 2010; Vesper and de Groot, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations and citations to earlier work.

claim: The dependence of the thermodynamic and kinetic properties on the box size is well within the level of statistical fluctuations for the observed statistics of 10–20 independent simulations at the microsecond timescale.
source: Our analyses show that the dependence of the thermodynamic and kinetic properties on the box size is well within the level of statistical fluctuations for the observed statistics of 10–20 independent simulations at the microsecond timescale.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations.

claim: The differences arising due to the different force fields, starting structures and chaotic nature of the simulations in this regime were found to be larger than the box size induced effects for the investigated systems.
source: The differences arising due to the different force fields, starting structures and chaotic nature of the simulations in this regime were found to be larger than the box size induced effects for the investigated systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' simulations.
